en: The Supreme Brahman, whose essential nature is established through the means of the collection of principles in the Śārīraka-Upaniṣad,
and who is to be known through the Śārīraka-Upaniṣad— that Śrī Rāma-Brahman is my refuge.
Oṃ. May He protect us both; may He nourish us both; may we work together with vigor;
may our study be brilliant; may we never harbor enmity toward one another.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace!
Oṃ. Now, therefore, the body is the combination of the great elements beginning with earth.
That which is solid is earth; that which is liquid is water; that which is hot is fire; that which moves is air; and that which is porous is space.
The sense organs of cognition are the ear and the others. The ear is in space, the skin in air, the eye in fire, the tongue in water, and the nose in earth.
Thus, these—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—are the objects of the sense organs in their respective order.
The objects [of the senses] arise sequentially within the great elements, beginning with earth.
The organs of action are known as speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ. Their respective objects are speaking, grasping, locomotion, excretion, and sexual pleasure.

The fourfold internal organ consists of mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*), which arise sequentially from the great elements beginning with earth.
Their respective natures are volition, conceptualization, determination, and self-identification.
The objects [of the senses] are as follows:
the throat is the seat of the mind (*manas*), the mouth of the intellect (*buddhi*), the heart of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), and the navel of the consciousness (*citta*).
Furthermore, bones, skin, channels, body hair, and flesh are the portions of earth.
Urine, phlegm, blood, semen, and sweat belong to the *avaṃśa* (the non-essential).
Hunger, thirst, laziness, delusion, and sexual intercourse belong to *agni* (fire).
Moving about, scraping, blinking the eyes, opening and closing them, and so forth, belong to *vāyu* (wind).
Desire, anger, greed, delusion, and fear belong to space.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the qualities of earth.
Sound, touch, form, and taste are the qualities of water.
Sound, touch, and form are the qualities of fire;
sound and touch are the qualities of air;
and sound alone is the quality of space.
The three qualities (guṇas) are characterized by the attributes of sattva, rajas, and tamas.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness;
freedom from anger, service to the teacher, purity, contentment, and straightforwardness. (1)
Humility, freedom from hypocrisy, faith in the scriptures, and non-violence—all these qualities are to be known as belonging especially to one characterized by sattva. || 2 ||
"I am the doer, I am the enjoyer, I am the speaker, and I possess self-conceit"—these qualities are declared by the best of the knowers of Brahman to belong to the rajasic person. (3)
Sleep, laziness, delusion, passion, sexual intercourse, and theft—these are declared by the exponents of Brahman to be the qualities of the tamasic nature. || 4 ||
Above is the *sāttvika*, in the middle is the *rājasa*, and below is the *tāmasa*.

Knowledge of truth is *sāttvika*; knowledge of duty is *rājasa*; and that which is blinded by darkness is *tāmasa*. Furthermore, there are four states: waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (*turīya*).
The waking state is characterized by the fourteen instruments consisting of the five organs of knowledge, the five organs of action, and the fourfold internal organ.
The dreaming state is joined with the fourfold internal organ alone. Deep sleep has the mind as its sole instrument.
The fourth state (turīya) is indeed that which is endowed with the pure soul alone.

Between the individual soul (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman)—the former being like the eye opened and the latter like the eye closed—the individual soul is known as the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).

The subtle body, composed of the five organs of cognition, the five organs of action, the five vital breaths, the mind, and the intellect— consisting thus of seventeen components— is called the *liṅga* (the indicative mark).
Mind, intellect, ego, ether, air, fire, water, and earth—these are the eight primary natures (prakṛtis); the other sixteen are the transformations (vikāras).
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth; the anus, the generative organ, the hands, the feet, and speech is considered the tenth. (7)
Sound, touch, form, taste, and likewise smell—
these twenty-three principles are indeed the manifest prakṛtis.
The twenty-fourth is the unmanifest Pradhāna, and beyond that is the Puruṣa.
Thus ends the Upaniṣad.
Oṃ. May He protect us both together; may He nourish us both together; may we work together with vigor;
may our study be brilliant; may we never have any enmity toward one another.
Oṃ. Peace, peace, peace.
Thus ends the Śārīraka Upaniṣad belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.
